elements.quote: Chronic psychological stress has been proposed as a contributor to metabolic dysfunction; however, evidence linking perceived stress to MetS and its individual components remains inconsistent.
elements.reason: Describes the current state of knowledge (proposed link) and an important uncertainty (evidence remains inconsistent), but does not clearly detail other specific uncertainties or gaps beyond inconsistency.

elements.quote: The Perceived Stress Scale (PSS) is a widely validated instrument for assessing subjective stress, yet its association with metabolic outcomes has not been systematically synthesised.
elements.reason: Explains the need for the review by stating that the association between perceived stress (measured by PSS) and metabolic outcomes has not yet been systematically synthesized.
No evidence in the retrieved text mentions similar systematic reviews or explains the need for this review in relation to prior reviews (including updates/replications).
The review is about the association between perceived stress and metabolic parameters, not an intervention effect; no proposed mechanism of an intervention is described in the retrieved evidence.
There is no indication of a complex intervention or delivery context in the retrieved evidence, and no logic model is presented.

elements.quote: The objective of this study was to systematically review the evidence and evaluate the association between perceived stress, measured using the PSS, and metabolic parameters related to MetS.
elements.reason: An objective is explicitly stated, but it is not clearly formulated as a review question using a relevant question-formulation framework (e.g., PICO/PEO/other).

elements.quote: The objective of this study was to systematically review the evidence and evaluate the association between perceived stress, measured using the PSS, and metabolic parameters related to MetS.
elements.reason: The review objective is to evaluate an association (perceived stress with metabolic parameters), not to provide planned comparisons of intervention effects using PICO or a variant.

elements.quote: Studies were eligible if they: (1) used an observational or interventional design reporting baseline associations; (2) enrolled adults aged ≥18 years; (3) assessed chronic psychological stress with PSS-10 or PSS-14; (4) reported MetS diagnosis or at least one metabolic component; and (5) provided sufficient data to derive effect estimates.
elements.reason: Eligibility specifies study designs, participant age, stress assessment instrument (PSS-10/PSS-14), metabolic outcomes, and data sufficiency. However, it does not clearly specify all relevant components such as settings and follow-up requirements.

elements.quote: Only studies published from 2015 onward were considered; this date threshold was determined to focus on evidence generated after widespread adoption of the PSS-10 as the dominant instrument in metabolic research, and is acknowledged as a limitation.
elements.reason: A dissemination-year restriction (published from 2015 onward) is specified, but there is no explicit specification of language or publication/report status (e.g., whether only peer-reviewed, inclusion of unpublished reports, etc.).
The evidence does not report a distinction between exclusions due to outcomes not being measured versus exclusions due to outcome results not being reported.
The evidence does not specify the groups used in each synthesis and how those groups are linked to the comparisons defined in the review objectives.

elements.quote: Data Preparation and Standardisation Although the PROSPERO protocol specified inclusion of studies using the PSS-10, studies employing the PSS-14 were also included to maximise available evidence. To ensure comparability across instruments, perceived stress scores were standardised using z-scores: z = (study PSS mean - overall PSS mean) / overall PSS SD, where the overall mean was 19.20 (SD = 9.48) across all 30 studies. Variance of the z-score was calculated using propagation of error: Var(z) = (study PSS SD)² / (sample size × overall PSS SD²).
elements.reason: The methods for data preparation/standardisation (PSS-10 vs PSS-14 inclusion and z-score conversion with variance calculation) are described, but there is no explicit description of handling missing summary statistics (e.g., missing SD/SE) beyond the available extraction/standardisation information.

elements.quote: Leave-one-out sensitivity analyses for the BMI meta-regression demonstrated stable results (beta coefficients ranging from 0.010 to 0.021 across iterations). Similar sensitivity analyses were conducted for other primary metabolic predictors, all showing consistent results. All meta-regression models were also re-run in the protocol-aligned direction (PSS z-score predicting each metabolic outcome); results were consistent and are reported in the supplemental material. For HOMA-IR, the leave-one-out analysis (supplemental material) showed that the association remained significant when Raja-Khan (2017) was omitted (k = 3: β = 2.072, 95% CI: 0.189-3.955, p = 0.045) but became non-significant when any of the other three studies (Berg-Schmidt, Tauqir, or Kautzky) was removed, confirming that this finding is exploratory and requires replication.

elements.quote: DISCUSSION ARTICLE IN PRESS Metabolic syndrome is a complex disorder characterised by a cluster of clinical and biochemical abnormalities that contribute to the early development of metabolic and cardiovascular diseases.¹ Its increasing global prevalence has expanded research beyond traditional risk factors, highlighting the role of non-classical determinants such as chronic psychological stress. These observations are consistent with the broader evidence base linking psychological stress to obesity and its cardiometabolic complications.¹⁰¹¹¹²⁹ Chronic stress represents a disruption of homeostasis induced by psychological, physiological, or environmental stimuli. While acute stress responses are adaptive, sustained activation of stress pathways leads to neurochemical, neuroanatomical, and cellular changes that adversely affect multiple physiological systems.¹² Central to this response is activation of the HPA axis and the sympathetic nervous system, resulting in increased cortisol secretion and catecholamine release.¹³ Glucocorticoids exert counter-regulatory effects on insulin, promoting gluconeogenesis, lipolysis, and energy storage.¹⁴ Cortisol preferentially stimulates visceral adipose tissue, which exhibits higher glucocorticoid receptor density than subcutaneous fat, contributing to central fat accumulation, increased free fatty acid release, and inflammatory signalling, all of which promote insulin resistance.¹⁵
elements.reason: The manuscript interprets the findings by relating them to the broader evidence base and proposing biologically plausible mechanisms (HPA axis, cortisol effects) consistent with prior research on psychological stress and cardiometabolic outcomes.

elements.quote: This study has several limitations. High heterogeneity across analyses reflects substantial variability in study design, populations, stress assessment, and covariate adjustment. I² exceeded 90% for most outcomes, and exploratory moderator analyses (by PSS version, study design, and clinical vs. general population) did not explain this heterogeneity appreciably; pooled estimates should therefore be regarded as hypothesis-generating. The predominance of cross-sectional studies limits causal inference, and the small number of studies available for certain metabolic predictors reduces statistical power. Residual confounding and publication bias cannot be entirely excluded. ARTICLE IN PRESS Although inclusion of both PSS-10 and PSS-14 enhanced study coverage, this may have contributed to between-study heterogeneity despite score standardisation. Consistent with these limitations, the overall certainty of evidence was rated as very low according to the GRADE framework.
elements.reason: The Discussion/Limitations section explicitly discusses limitations of the evidence included in the review, including heterogeneity, cross-sectional design limiting causality, limited study numbers reducing power, residual confounding and publication bias, and very low certainty of evidence (GRADE).
